senses.definition: Based on hypothesis and theory rather than experiment or empirical evidence.
senses.example: In his opening argument, the student mentioned nothing beyond his a priori knowledge.

senses.definition: Self-evident, intuitively obvious.
Presumed without analysis.
Developed entirely from scratch, without deriving it from existing languages.
In a way based on theoretical deduction rather than empirical observation.

core.definition: Known or reasoned from general principles before observation, deduced from theory rather than tested by experience.

pronunciation.tip: The given British style 'ah pree-OR-ee' is not standard American speech. Say 'ay pry-OR-eye' with stress on OR and a clear, rhotic r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy and mathematics; it can sound dismissive when used of an unexamined assumption.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this Latin term in philosophy, mathematics, economics and statistics, often with a prior assumption or prior probability. In everyday speech they say 'in principle' or 'without checking' instead. Describing an assumption as a priori suggests it was never tested, which can sound critical in meetings.

distinctions.note: A priori reasoning starts from principles before experience; a posteriori reasoning starts from observed facts.
Innate describes what a person is born with; a priori describes knowledge justified by reason, whether or not it is innate.
Prior means earlier in time or order; a priori is a philosophical term for knowledge that does not depend on experience.

examples.everyday: Don't just assume the pharmacy's open on Sunday; that's an a priori guess, so check the hours.
examples.professional: We shouldn't make an a priori assumption that customers want the new feature; let's run a quick test first.
examples.analytical: Kant argued that space and time are a priori forms of intuition, not concepts learned from experience.

nuance.analogy: Like knowing that a triangle's angles add to 180 degrees before measuring any actual triangle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin a priori, 'from the earlier', from prior, meaning earlier.
common_mistakes: Using it casually to mean 'in advance', when the term has a precise philosophical meaning.
Pronouncing it as 'ah pree-OR-ee', which is the wrong vowel and stress for American English.

core.definition: A mountain range east of the Jordan River in Moab, including Mount Nebo, from which Moses viewed the Promised Land.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, pronounce the first vowel as the short a in cat, and make the middle syllable a reduced schwa. The r is clear and rhotic, so it is not 'Abb-uh-reem'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a geographic name with strong religious associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear Abarim mostly in Bible study, church, or travel to Jordan and Israel. Most people refer to the peak Mount Nebo instead. A natural reply in church is 'Yes, that's where Moses looked over the land he could not enter.'

distinctions.note: Nebo is the peak within the Abarim range where Moses is said to have died; Abarim names the whole range.
Pisgah is a summit of the range that appears in Deuteronomy as a place of view over the land.
Moab is the country and plateau east of the Dead Sea; Abarim is the mountain range within or above that area.

examples.everyday: Our pastor showed a photo of the view from the Abarim mountains, where Moses saw the Promised Land.
examples.professional: The Abarim ridge overlooks the Jordan Valley, so our tour group planned the photo stops there.
examples.analytical: Numbers 27 presents Abarim as the place from which Moses views the land he will not enter, marking his exclusion from the conquest.

nuance.analogy: Like a lookout ridge above a valley you are not allowed to enter.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ha-'Avarim, meaning the regions across, from the root 'avar, to cross over.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'uh-BAR-im'.
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'ay' or 'ah' rather than the short a in cat.
nuance.biblical_note: Abarim is the range of mountains east of the Jordan from which Moses sees the Promised Land before his death. In Numbers 27:12, the Lord tells Moses to go up into the mountain of Abarim and look over the land. Deuteronomy 32:49 places Mount Nebo in the Abarim range, and Deuteronomy 34:1 describes Moses going up from the plains of Moab to Nebo, the top of Pisgah. The passages show Moses' view of the land as a sign of his exclusion from entering it.

senses.definition: To touch by means of a mutual border, edge or end; to border on; to lie adjacent (to); to be contiguous (said of an area of land)
senses.example: It was a time when Germany still abutted upon Russia.

senses.definition: To border upon; be next to; abut on; be adjacent to.
To lean against on one end; to end on, of a part of a building or wall.

core.definition: To touch or share a border with something; to be next to it or lean directly against it along an edge.

pronunciation.tip: The single syllable is stressed, so the final t is a clear, unflapped sound, as in 'but' with a crisp stop. Do not pronounce it as 'uh-BUH' or as 'a-BET'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and descriptive, used for property lines and physical boundaries.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'abut' mainly in real estate, surveying, legal descriptions, and city planning, as in 'the lot abuts the park'. In everyday speech, they say 'borders' or 'is right next to'. Use it in writing when you want precision, but avoid it in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Border is common and everyday; abut stresses direct contact along a shared edge, usually in technical or legal writing.
Adjoin means to be connected to something next to it; abut is slightly more specific about a shared boundary.

collocations: a property that abuts the river

examples.everyday: My backyard abuts the school field, so we hear the recess noise all day.
examples.professional: The proposed warehouse abuts the residential zone, so the city will require a buffer strip.
examples.analytical: The legal description states that the easement abuts the western boundary and runs for two hundred feet.

nuance.analogy: Like two puzzle pieces that touch along one clean edge without overlapping.
nuance.etymology: From Old French abouter 'to touch at the end', from a- 'to' plus bout 'end, extremity'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'abut to the wall'; the correct structures are 'abut on' or 'abut against'.
Confusing 'abut' with 'abet' (to help), which is pronounced similarly but means something different.

abut.etymology: From Middle English *abutten*, from Medieval Latin *abuttare* and Old French *abuter*, *aboter*, *abouter* (“to touch at one end, to come to an end, aim, reach”), from Old French *but* (“end, aim, purpose”); akin to.

senses.definition: An instance of admixing, a mixing in of something.
senses.example: The admixture of vanilla extract in the dough improved the pastries' flavor.

senses.definition: A mixing-in of a biologically or genetically differentiated group to an established stock.
A mixture, in some contexts:
senses.example: Background EEG demonstrates an admixture of theta and delta waves.

senses.definition: A mixture composed of entities retaining their individual properties.
senses.example: Background EEG demonstrates an admixture of theta and delta waves.

core.definition: A mixture, or something mixed into a substance or group to create a blend.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MIX, the second syllable. The 'ks' cluster is one crisp sound, and the ending is 'chur,' not 'cha.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds technical or literary, and when used for people or populations it must be handled with care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use admixture in everyday talk; it appears in science, genetics, medicine, and formal writing. 'Mix' or 'blend' is the everyday equivalent. In genetics, admixture describes mixing between populations, which can sound sensitive when applied to people, so use the term precisely and carefully.

distinctions.note: Mixture is the everyday general word; admixture usually means a substance or element added into something else, often in technical contexts.
Blend suggests a smooth, harmonious combination; admixture focuses on the thing being added.
An alloy is a specific metal mixture; admixture is broader and can apply to any substance or population.

examples.everyday: This coffee has a strange admixture of cinnamon and orange peel, but I kind of like it.
examples.professional: The lab protocol specifies a small admixture of the catalyst before the mix is heated.
examples.analytical: Her argument depends on separating genuine historical influence from the admixture of later additions to the texts.

nuance.analogy: Like adding a spoon of vinegar to a pot of soup: a small addition that changes the whole taste.
nuance.etymology: From Latin admiscere 'to mix in,' from ad- 'to' plus miscere 'to mix.'
common_mistakes: Using 'admixture' in casual speech where 'mix' is more natural
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'cha' or stressing the first syllable

admixture.etymology: From Latin *admixtūra*, from *admixtus*, past participle of *admisceō* (“to mix in”), from *misceō* (“to mix”).

senses.definition: To inform or notify of a fault; to rebuke in a serious tone; to tell off.
To advise against wrongdoing; to caution; to warn against danger or an offense.
To instruct or direct.

core.definition: To warn or scold someone firmly, often gently but seriously, about a mistake or bad behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAHN, the second syllable, and the first vowel is a reduced schwa, not 'ad.' The 'o' in the stressed syllable is the American 'ah' sound, as in 'cot.'

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly negative. It implies disapproval, though it is usually less harsh than 'scold' or 'reprimand.'
nuance.usage_note: Admonish is formal and slightly old-fashioned in American speech. You will hear it more in writing, news, or religious texts than in casual talk. Americans usually say 'warn,' 'tell off,' or 'chew out' informally. A natural reply is 'Got it, I'll be more careful.'

distinctions.note: Warn means alert someone to a danger or future problem; admonish means to scold or caution someone about behavior they already showed.
A reprimand is usually a formal, official rebuke, often at work; admonish can be gentler and more personal.
Scold is informal and emotional and is often used for children; admonish is more formal and calmer.

examples.everyday: My mom admonished me for leaving the lights on, but she was smiling when she said it.
examples.professional: The manager admonished the team to file expense reports on time, and the message was clearly a warning.
examples.analytical: Paul admonishes the Corinthians not to divide into factions, grounding his appeal in their shared identity in Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach pulling a player aside at halftime to correct a mistake, firmly but without anger.
nuance.etymology: From Old French amonester, from Latin admonere 'to warn, remind,' from ad- plus monere 'to advise, warn.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'admonish me to' when you mean 'admonish me for' the offense
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'ad' instead of the reduced 'uh'

senses.definition: Exhibiting adulation; overly flattering.
senses.example: adulatory comments

core.definition: Excessively praising or flattering someone, often in a way that seems insincere or designed to win favor.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, AJ, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced. Say the final -ory as 'ree' with a clear American r, and don't add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling praise adulatory suggests it is excessive and probably insincere, so it is an unflattering word to use about someone's own compliments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adulatory mostly in writing, journalism, and formal commentary about politics, celebrity, or media coverage. In conversation people usually say 'over the top' or 'fawning' instead. It is not a casual word, and using it in small talk would sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Sycophantic describes a person who flatters to gain favor; adulatory describes the praise itself, which may be excessive but not necessarily aimed at personal gain.
Complimentary is neutral or positive and fits everyday praise; adulatory is much stronger and implies praise has gone too far.

examples.everyday: My brother gave his new boss such an adulatory speech at dinner that we all started laughing.
examples.professional: The quarterly newsletter was so adulatory about the product launch that our analysts didn't trust a word of it.
examples.analytical: The biography's adulatory portrait of the general ignores the evidence of his failures, which makes its historical claims difficult to accept.

nuance.analogy: Like a cheerleader who never stops shouting, adulatory praise is loud and constant enough to stop sounding sincere.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adulatorius, from adulari 'to fawn upon, flatter'.
common_mistakes: Using adulatory to mean simply 'positive' or 'kind'; it implies excess and insincerity.
Stressing the wrong syllable as ad-yoo-LAY-tor-ee; the stress belongs on the first syllable, AJ.

senses.definition: The act or process of collecting in a mass; a heaping together.
A state of being collected in a mass; a mass; a cluster.
An extended city area comprising the built-up area of a central city and any suburbs linked by continuous urban area.
A mass of large volcanic fragments bonded under heat.

core.definition: A large, dense collection or mass of things or people, or a city together with its surrounding suburbs.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on -AY-, the syllable before -shun, and the 'mer' syllable is reduced to a light 'mer' sound. Keep the stress off the first syllable, which is weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term for a large cluster, sometimes with a slightly impersonal tone when used for cities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in urban planning, economics, and geography to refer to a metropolitan area or a dense cluster of firms. In everyday speech they say 'a big cluster of stores' or 'the metro area'. It is rarely used casually.

distinctions.note: 'Aggregation' often means combining data or totals, while 'agglomeration' emphasizes that the parts physically gather into a dense mass.
'Cluster' is an everyday word for a small group; 'agglomeration' is more formal and often refers to a large urban or industrial area.
'Conurbation' is a British-style term for a continuous urban area; Americans more often say 'metropolitan area' or 'metro area'.

examples.everyday: Houston is a huge agglomeration, so driving across town during rush hour takes forever.
examples.professional: Our site-selection report shows that the Austin agglomeration offers better talent and lower logistics costs.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that agglomeration effects explain why firms in the same industry cluster in certain cities despite high rents.

nuance.analogy: Like a crowd of people drawn to the same concert, which becomes denser and larger as more people arrive.
nuance.etymology: From Latin agglomeratio, from agglomerare 'to wind onto a ball'.
common_mistakes: Using 'agglomeration' for any group of things in casual speech, where 'cluster' or 'group' is more natural.
Confusing it with 'aggregation' when the meaning is physical clumping rather than totals.

core.definition: A family or clan designation, apparently from an ancestor named Ahoah, used in the Bible for two of David's warriors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HOH. The final syllable rhymes with light, and the first syllable is a reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term from biblical genealogy.
nuance.usage_note: This is a Bible term used in study, commentary, and translation discussions. Americans rarely use it outside those contexts. It is a gentilic, a form that names a family or origin, similar to Hittite or Netophathite.
collocations: Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group got stuck on the word Ahohite, so we looked it up in a commentary.
examples.professional: In the lesson on David's mighty men, I explain that Ahohite marks a family name rather than a place.
examples.analytical: The gentilic Ahohite in 2 Samuel 23 identifies Eleazar's father by clan, which tells us the lists were arranged by kinship as well as by achievement.

nuance.analogy: Like a family crest attached to a name, telling you where a person's line comes from without giving a street address.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew family name Aḥôaḥ, apparently an ancestor mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:4; the derivation is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Treating the word as a place name rather than a family designation.
Stressing the last syllable, as in uh-HOH-HITE.
nuance.biblical_note: The term Ahohite appears in 2 Samuel 23:9, where Eleazar is called the son of Dodo the Ahohite, and in 1 Chronicles 11:12 with the same name. Zalmon the Ahohite is named in 2 Samuel 23:28 among David's warriors. The word marks clan or family identity inside the lists of David's mighty men.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the medieval chemical science and philosophy of alchemy.
Of or pertaining to an unexplainable transmutation.
Of or pertaining to the creation of something special out of a common material.

core.definition: Relating to alchemy, the medieval study of transforming matter, or describing a mysterious transformation.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MIH, the third syllable, with a lighter stress on AL at the start. The final syllable is weak, so say 'kul' with a reduced vowel. Don't add an extra syllable between 'mih' and 'kul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical and scholarly contexts; positive when used figuratively to praise a mysterious or remarkable transformation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'alchemical' mainly in history of science, philosophy, religious studies, and literature, and in figurative praise like 'alchemical process.' In everyday speech, people more often say 'magical' or 'transformative.' It is a precise scholarly adjective, so use it when discussing historical alchemy or a clearly metaphorical transformation.

distinctions.note: 'Alchemic' is a less common variant; 'alchemical' is the standard adjective in most scholarly writing.
'Magical' suggests fantasy or wonder; 'alchemical' specifically refers to alchemy or to a transformation that seems to change base matter into something valuable.

examples.everyday: The way the chef turned leftover bread into something amazing was almost alchemical.
examples.professional: The team's alchemical approach to turning messy data into a clean feature set impressed the leadership.
examples.analytical: Jung read the alchemical texts as symbolic accounts of psychological transformation, not as failed chemistry.

nuance.analogy: An alchemical change is like turning a rough sketch into a finished painting: something common becomes valuable through a process.
nuance.etymology: From 'alchemy' plus the adjective suffix '-ical,' from Medieval Latin 'alchimia' and Arabic 'al-kīmiyā.'
common_mistakes: Using 'alchemical' to mean 'chemical' in ordinary science talk.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'al-KEM-ih-kul'.
Confusing it with 'alchemic,' which is less common in standard writing.

core.definition: The name of several Old Testament men, most notably a chief priest under King Jehoshaphat and an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, RY, and say the final syllable as a weak uh. The name is often mispronounced with stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name found in religious reading and genealogy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Amariah in Bible reading, Old Testament study, and sermons on the priesthood or prophets. Outside religion the name is rarely used, though it is a real first name in some families. Saying Amariah in a casual talk would usually mean you are discussing a biblical person.

distinctions.note: Amaziah was a king of Judah, while Amariah was a priest and a name in several genealogies, so the two names refer to different people.
Mariah is a common modern first name, while Amariah is an Old Testament name with the same ending but a different origin.

examples.everyday: During our Bible study we read about a priest named Amariah in Chronicles, and nobody had heard of him before.
examples.professional: The genealogy in Ezra lists Amariah, so the name matters for tracing priestly families in the postexilic period.
examples.analytical: In 2 Chronicles 19:11, Amariah is appointed chief priest over matters concerning the Lord, which reflects the Chronicler's picture of reform under Jehoshaphat.

nuance.analogy: Amariah is like a name on a family tree that appears in several branches, so you need the context to know which one is meant.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Amaryah, meaning roughly Yahweh has promised or Yahweh has spoken.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in AM-uh-ryah, instead of am-uh-RY-uh.
Pronouncing the final syllable as ee, as in am-uh-RY-ee, instead of a weak uh.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name 'Amaryah (עֲמַרְיָה) probably means Yahweh has promised or Yahweh has spoken, and it belongs to several men in the Old Testament. 2 Chronicles 19:11 names Amariah the chief priest, who is given authority over matters of the Lord during Jehoshaphat's reign. Zephaniah 1:1 traces the prophet Zephaniah back through four generations, and Ezra 7:3 includes Amariah in the genealogy of Ezra the scribe.

senses.definition: Wrong; faulty; out of order; improper or otherwise incorrect.
senses.example: He suspected something was amiss.

senses.definition: Astray.
Imperfectly.

core.definition: Wrong or not as it should be; something that is off or not right in a situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable clearly: uh-MISS, with a short 'i' like 'miss', not a long 'ee'. The first syllable is weak.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests something is wrong, usually in a subtle or unclear way rather than a dramatic problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use amiss mostly in the set phrases 'something is amiss' or 'nothing is amiss', often in writing or formal storytelling. In everyday speech people more often say 'something's off' or 'something's wrong'. Be careful: 'take it amiss' means to be offended, which is a different phrase.

distinctions.note: Wrong is direct and stronger; amiss is softer and more literary, usually used after a verb like 'seem' or 'be'.
Off is casual spoken American, as in 'something feels off'; amiss is more formal and written.

examples.everyday: Something seems amiss with the dishwasher; it's not draining at all.
examples.professional: Nothing looked amiss in the logs, but the totals still didn't match the invoices.
examples.analytical: The argument is not wholly amiss, but it ignores the historical context that makes the policy intelligible.

nuance.analogy: A picture hung slightly crooked: nothing is broken, but something is not quite right.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English amis, from Old French a mes, roughly 'at fault'.
common_mistakes: Placing amiss before a noun ('an amiss result'); it normally comes after a verb.
Confusing take it amiss (be offended) with something is amiss (something is wrong).

senses.definition: The moment in the plot of a drama in which the hero makes a discovery that explains previously unexplained events or situations; a denouement.

core.definition: In a drama, the moment when a character discovers a crucial truth, often about identity or relationships, that explains earlier events and changes the plot.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NAHR, the open a of cot, and the g is hard, not silent. Say the cluster 'ag-n' by moving quickly from the g to the n, and keep the last syllable short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in literary analysis, where it marks a turning point. In casual speech, the idea is simply a big reveal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use anagnorisis in literature classes, drama criticism, and discussions of Aristotle's Poetics. In everyday talk, people would say 'the big reveal', 'the moment everything clicked', or 'the turning point'. The term is precise but academic, so use it when analyzing a story, not when recounting a movie to friends.

distinctions.note: Peripeteia is a sudden reversal of fortune, while anagnorisis is the moment of recognition or discovery that often triggers that reversal.
A plot twist is a casual term for any surprise in a story, while anagnorisis is a specific dramatic moment of recognition, usually about identity.

examples.everyday: When the mechanic turned out to be the brother she'd lost years ago, that was pure anagnorisis for the whole family.
examples.professional: In the case study, the anagnorisis came when the client realized the revenue data had been mislabeled from the start.
examples.analytical: In Oedipus Rex, the anagnorisis arrives when Oedipus discovers that he is the killer he has been hunting, and the revelation reshapes every earlier scene.

nuance.analogy: Like a light switch that suddenly illuminates the whole room, showing what was already there but unseen.
nuance.etymology: From Greek anagnōrisis, 'recognition' or 'discovery', from ana- 'again' plus gnōrizein 'to know'.
common_mistakes: Using anagnorisis as a synonym for any surprise, when it means a specific moment of recognition.
Confusing it with peripeteia, which is the reversal of fortune rather than the discovery itself.
Pronouncing the g as silent, or stressing the wrong syllable.

senses.definition: The act of annunciating.

core.definition: The angel Gabriel's announcement to Mary that she would conceive and bear Jesus; also the church feast commemorating it, March 25.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AY, the fourth syllable from the start. The 'ci' is pronounced 'see' (not 'sh'), and the first syllable is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent in religious use; neutral as a general word for a formal announcement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always capitalize it (the Annunciation) and mean the biblical event or the feast day. It is common in church settings and art history, and many churches are named Annunciation. The general sense 'a formal announcement' is rare; Americans say announcement.

distinctions.note: Announcement is the everyday word for any public statement; Annunciation usually refers to Gabriel's message to Mary.
Enunciation means clear pronunciation of words, not announcing news.
The Annunciation is the message; the Incarnation is the Son of God becoming human, traditionally begun at Mary's conception of Jesus.

examples.everyday: We go to Annunciation Church on Greek Easter, and the feast in March is a big day for them.
examples.professional: This week's lecture will compare Renaissance depictions of the Annunciation in Florence and Siena.
examples.analytical: In Luke's account, the Annunciation joins divine initiative and Mary's free response, a pairing that later Marian theology developed at length.

nuance.analogy: Like a royal herald's proclamation, but delivered by an angel to one young woman.
nuance.etymology: From Latin annuntiatio, 'announcement,' from annuntiare, 'to announce' (ad- 'to' + nuntius 'messenger').
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'ci' as 'sh' (uh-nun-SHAY-shun) instead of 'see'.
Using it for any ordinary announcement; use announcement.
nuance.biblical_note: The event is told in Luke 1:26-38: the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son named Jesus, and she answers in humble acceptance. Gabriel's earlier announcement of John the Baptist's birth to Zechariah is in Luke 1:11-20. Matthew 1:20-21 has a related angelic message to Joseph. The Greek verb euangelizo ('to bring good news') is related in spirit.

annunciation.etymology: From Middle English *annunciacion*, *annunciation*, from Latin *annuntiātiō* and Old French *anonciacion*.

senses.definition: Invites the audience to ask questions.

core.definition: A phrase a presenter or meeting leader uses to invite the audience or participants to ask questions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWES in 'questions', and the 'tch' sound is a single quick 'ch' before 'uhnz'. In fast speech 'any' reduces to 'nee', so keep the second syllable light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it signals openness and a wish for engagement.
nuance.usage_note: Presenters say this at the end of a talk or after a section, usually with a rising tone and a short pause. Americans often follow it with 'Go ahead' or by naming someone to call on. Common replies are 'Yes, on slide six' or 'I have one quick question.' A shorter, more casual version is simply 'Questions?'.

distinctions.note: Shorter and more casual, with the same invitation; very common in American meetings.
More complete and slightly more formal; suits presentations to clients or large groups.

examples.everyday: Okay, that's the recipe. Any questions before we head out to the store?
examples.professional: That covers the rollout plan. Any questions before we move on to the budget?
examples.analytical: Any questions? is less an open invitation than a closing ritual, one that signals the speaker's authority over the content and tests whether anyone will challenge it.

nuance.analogy: Like a host asking if anyone needs anything before the party gets going.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'questions' with a hard t sound instead of the American 'ch' sound in 'KWES-chuhnz'.
Saying 'Have you any questions?' which sounds stiff and British in American meetings.

conversation.text: That's all I have. Any questions?
Before we move on, are there any questions?
If there are any questions, feel free to email me.

senses.definition: At any time.
senses.example: I don’t like beer much. Give me a fine wine anytime.

senses.definition: A form of you're welcome in response to thank you or thanks.
senses.example: Thanks so much for looking after Grandpa. — That’s all right. Any time, dawg.

senses.definition: Suitable for any time; not associated with any particular time.

core.definition: A friendly reply to 'thank you' meaning 'you're welcome' or 'I'm glad to help, any time you need.'

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the first syllable (EH), with a lighter second syllable (tyme). Do not stress the second word as in 'any TIME', which sounds like a separate phrase.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm; it signals a friendly, open offer to help again.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Anytime!' casually to friends, coworkers, and people who helped them. It is less suited to very formal settings or to strangers in serious situations, where 'You're welcome' or 'My pleasure' fits better. Say it with a smile so it sounds like a friendly offer rather than a brush-off.

distinctions.note: Standard and neutral, suitable in every setting.
Casual and common in service and friendly talk, though it can sound dismissive after a big favor.
Formal and warm, a courteous choice in restaurants or professional contexts.

examples.everyday: Thanks for picking up the kids today. Anytime, really.
examples.professional: Thanks for reviewing the deck so fast. Anytime, and let me know if you want another pass.
examples.analytical: Anytime turns gratitude into a standing offer, implying that the favor could be repeated without cost, ceremony, or a formal request.

nuance.analogy: Like a door left unlocked: the offer stands whenever you come back.
nuance.etymology: From 'any' (Old English 'ænig') and 'time', combined into one word in the reply sense.
common_mistakes: Writing 'any time' as two words when you mean the friendly reply; the one-word form is the standard reply in speech and informal writing.
Answering a sincere, serious apology with 'Anytime', which can sound flippant; 'That's okay' fits better.

anytime.etymology: From Middle English *any time*, *ony tyme*, from Old English *ǣniġum tīman*, equivalent to *any* + *time*.

conversation.text: "Thanks for listening." "Anytime. You know where to find me."
Call me anytime if you need something.
We can meet up anytime next week.

senses.definition: Void of feeling; not susceptible of deep emotion.
Of, or pertaining to apatheism.
An apathetic or indifferent person, especially one who shows no interest in a particular issue.

core.definition: Showing little or no interest, enthusiasm, or concern about something, often because you do not care.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on THET, and the final syllable is a short 'ik', not 'eek'. The first vowel is a short a as in 'cat', and learners often wrongly stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies a lack of care and can sound judgmental, so use it carefully about people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to describe people who do not care about school, politics, or work, often in news, reviews, and essays. It can sound harsh when applied to a friend, so casual speakers often say 'I don't care' or 'I'm just over it'. A common phrase in American news is 'apathetic voters'.

distinctions.note: Neutral and general; apathetic suggests a lasting lack of motivation or feeling, not just lack of preference.
Plainer and more everyday; apathetic is stronger and implies a persistent disengagement.
Specific to effort; apathetic is broader and includes emotional disengagement.

examples.everyday: My little brother seems totally apathetic about college, so I'm not sure he'll apply anywhere.
examples.professional: Leadership worried the team had become apathetic about the new process after months of missed targets.
examples.analytical: Apathetic describes a condition of diminished concern, which differs from deliberate detachment, since the apathetic person has ceased to care rather than chosen not to.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone on silent that nobody checks anymore.
nuance.etymology: From apathy, from Greek apatheia, meaning without feeling.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am apathetic' when you mean 'I am bored' or 'I am tired', since the word implies a broader lack of care.
Spelling it 'apathic' by analogy with other words; the correct spelling is apathetic.

conversation.text: A lot of young people feel apathetic about voting.
I've been so apathetic about cooking lately; we just order takeout.
The students seemed apathetic during the lecture.

senses.definition: Following a noun or noun phrase: by, for, or to each one; each by itself.
senses.example: These melons cost a dollar apiece.

core.definition: Each; for or to each one of a group, considered separately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PEES. The first syllable is a reduced 'uh,' and the vowel in 'pees' is a long clear 'ee,' not 'ih.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain counting or sharing word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apiece after a noun or number, as in 'two dollars apiece' or 'a slice apiece,' especially when talking about prices, shares and food. Before a noun, Americans usually say 'each,' as in 'each slice cost two dollars.' 'Apiece' is natural in everyday conversation, in shopping and when splitting a bill.

distinctions.note: Each usually comes before the noun ('each ticket'), while apiece comes after it ('two tickets apiece').
Per is more formal or technical and is common in price and rate phrases such as 'five dollars per person,' while apiece is more natural in casual speech.

examples.everyday: The waiter brought two tacos apiece, which was plenty for both of us.
examples.professional: Each team member gets two laptops apiece for the pilot, so please log the serial numbers.
examples.analytical: Joshua 4:8 records twelve stones set up as a memorial, which interpreters often read as one for each tribe apiece.

nuance.analogy: Apiece is like handing out cookies from a plate: each person gets the same number, and the amount is counted separately for each one.
nuance.etymology: From a- (on, to) plus piece.
common_mistakes: Putting 'apiece' before the noun, as in 'apiece ticket'; it normally follows the noun or number.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'AH-pees'; the stress is on the second syllable.

senses.definition: Deeming an assertion to be true because of the position or the authority of the person asserting it.

core.definition: A flawed argument that a claim must be true because a respected or powerful person says so, rather than because of evidence.

pronunciation.tip: The stresses fall on PEEL and THOR. In fast speech 'to' reduces to 'tuh', and 'authority' has weak first and last syllables, so it sounds like 'uh-THOR-uh-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in an argument, since the speaker is calling out weak reasoning; neutral as a logical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in logic classes, debates, and critical-thinking discussions to point out a weak argument, as in 'That's an appeal to authority.' It is not always a fallacy, because real experts in their field are good evidence; the problem arises when the authority is irrelevant or the claim is supported only by who said it. In casual talk people often just say 'because the expert said so.'

distinctions.note: The two phrases describe the same fallacy; argument from authority is the more traditional philosophical name, while appeal to authority is more common in logic courses.
Citing a true expert in their field is legitimate evidence; the fallacy appears when the authority is irrelevant, unqualified, or the argument rests only on who said it.

collocations: fall into an appeal to authority
logical fallacy such as an appeal to authority

examples.everyday: Stop saying it's true just because your uncle said so. That's an appeal to authority.
examples.professional: The vendor's slide just says a famous analyst endorsed the product, which is an appeal to authority, not proof.
examples.analytical: Locke's critique of argument from respect for authority insists that reason, not inherited opinion, must justify belief.

nuance.analogy: Like a sales clerk saying trust me because the manager said so: the claim may be true, but the reason is missing.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin argumentum ad verecundiam, argument to respect or modesty, a name used in logic since Locke.
common_mistakes: Assuming every appeal to an expert is a fallacy; relevant expertise is legitimate evidence.
Using the phrase for any mention of a famous person; the fallacy requires using authority in place of reasons.

senses.definition: To determine the value or worth of (something), particularly as a person appointed for this purpose.
senses.example: to appraise goods and chattels

senses.definition: To consider comprehensively.
To judge the performance of someone, especially a worker.
senses.example: At the end of the contract, you will be appraised by your line manager.

senses.definition: To estimate; to conjecture.
To praise; to commend.
To apprise, inform.

core.definition: To assess the value, quality, or performance of something or someone, often in a formal or expert way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The final z is voiced, like the sound at the end of 'buzz', not an s sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds businesslike and precise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'appraise' mainly for property, objects, and business, and sometimes for reviewing employee performance. In casual speech, people say 'value,' 'check out,' or 'look at' instead. 'The house was appraised at four hundred thousand dollars' is natural, but 'I appraised my friend's cooking' sounds stiff.

distinctions.note: 'Evaluate' is broader and fits any judgment of quality, while 'appraise' specifically suggests judging monetary or practical worth.
'Estimate' means roughly guessing a number or amount, while 'appraise' implies a careful, expert judgment of value.

examples.everyday: My uncle came over to appraise the old truck before he decided to buy it.
examples.professional: The bank will appraise the building before it approves the loan.
examples.analytical: Before appraising the argument, the reader must decide what the author counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a judge at a cooking contest, weighing each dish against a clear standard.
nuance.etymology: From Old French aprisier, from Latin appretiare, 'to set a price', from pretium, 'price'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'appraise' with 'apprise', which is a different verb meaning to inform someone.
Pronouncing it 'uh-PRAYS' with an s ending instead of a voiced z.

appraise.etymology: From Middle English *apreisen*, from Old French *aprisier* (“apraise, set a price on”), from Late Latin *appretio*, from *ad-* + Latin *pretium* (“price, value”) (English *precious*), from which also, a doublet.

senses.definition: A mystery or deep secret.
An elixir or secret remedy.

core.definition: A deep mystery or secret, usually something known only to a select few; in older usage, a secret remedy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and reduce the final syllable to a quick 'um' sound. The r is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive, suggesting mystery and special knowledge; it is rare and can sound pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use arcanum in speech. It appears in literature, historical writing, religious and philosophical texts, and occasionally in formal prose. For everyday talk, use 'secret' or 'mystery' instead. The plural is arcana.

distinctions.note: Secret is common in everyday English, while arcanum is formal and suggests deep, esoteric knowledge.
Mystery can be a puzzle or unsolved problem, while arcanum implies hidden knowledge reserved for insiders.

examples.professional: The old engineer treated the legacy code as an arcanum that only he could safely touch.
examples.analytical: The author treats the nature of the soul as an arcanum, a truth veiled from ordinary reason and revealed only through faith.

nuance.analogy: An arcanum is like a sealed letter: the message is real, but only the intended reader can open it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin arcanum, meaning 'secret thing', the neuter of arcanus, 'secret'.
common_mistakes: Using arcanum in everyday conversation, where 'secret' sounds more natural.
Using 'arcana' for a single item; the singular is arcanum.

senses.definition: To sprinkle or scatter (liquid or dust).
To falsely or maliciously charge someone.

core.definition: To publicly attack someone's reputation with false or damaging claims.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the vowel is the r-colored 'er' sound of 'bird.' The final s is a plain s, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes damaging attacks on someone's good name.
nuance.usage_note: Asperse is a formal and fairly rare verb used mainly in writing, journalism, and legal or academic discussion. Americans are more likely to say 'smear,' 'slander,' or 'badmouth' in everyday speech. Using it in casual conversation may sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Slander refers specifically to spoken false statements that harm reputation, and it is a legal term. Asperse is broader and can apply to written or spoken attacks.
Defame is a more legal or formal term for damaging someone's reputation with false statements. Asperse is more literary and less specific about the legal sense.

examples.everyday: I don't want to hear you asperse your coworker just because he got the promotion.
examples.professional: The blog post aspersed the engineer's work without showing any evidence, and HR asked for a correction.
examples.analytical: Critics who asperse an author's motives without engaging the arguments reduce public debate to personal attack.

nuance.analogy: Like throwing mud on a clean wall, where the mud can stain the surface even if it is later washed away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aspergere, meaning to sprinkle or scatter, from ad- and spargere, to scatter.
common_mistakes: Using it for sprinkling liquids in everyday contexts, when 'sprinkle' is the natural word.
Confusing it with 'aspire,' which has a different meaning and a different stress pattern.
Using it as a noun, when the noun is 'aspersion.'

senses.definition: The puff of air accompanying the release of a plosive or fricative consonant.
A sound produced by such a puff of air.
A mark of aspiration (ʽ) used in Greek; the asper, or rough breathing.
A sample of fluid, tissue, or other substance that is withdrawn via aspiration (usually through a hollow needle) from a body cavity, cyst, or tumor.
To remove a liquid or gas by means of suction.
To inhale something other than air into one's lungs.
To suffocate, having inhaled something other than air.
senses.example: The autopsy found that the casualty had aspirated in her sleep.

senses.definition: To produce an audible puff of breath, especially following a consonant, such as the letter "h" at the beginning of house or hat in standard English.
Synonym of aspirated.

core.definition: In phonetics, a puff of breath released with a consonant, as in the sound of p in 'pin' or t in 'top.'

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, AS, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel. Learners often pronounce the middle as 'pa-ray' when it should be a reduced 'puh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in linguistics and phonetics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aspirate mainly in linguistics, phonetics, speech therapy, or language teaching. Outside those areas it would sound unusual, and most speakers would not know the word. The verb form, pronounced AS-per-ayt, is used in medicine and cooking for removing liquid by suction, but the noun here is phonetic.

distinctions.note: Aspirate in the phonetic sense is the puff of air itself, while aspiration is the process of producing it or the broader term in phonetics.
Aspirated is the adjective describing a sound, as in an aspirated p. Aspirate as a noun names the puff of air.

examples.everyday: My teacher said that English p has a strong aspirate when it starts a word, like in 'pot.'
examples.professional: The speech recognition model struggled with the aspirate in the recordings, so we added more training examples.
examples.analytical: The phonological analysis treats the aspirate as a contrastive feature that distinguishes meaning in certain Korean word pairs.

nuance.analogy: Like a small puff of breath you feel on your hand when you say 'pop' close to your palm.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aspiratus, past participle of aspirare, meaning to breathe upon.
common_mistakes: Using the verb pronunciation for the noun, or stressing the wrong syllable.
Confusing it with 'aspiration,' which means strong desire in everyday use.
Assuming every consonant has an aspirate, when English only aspirates some voiceless stops at the start of stressed syllables.

senses.definition: One of the parallel attention operations in multi-head attention.

core.definition: One of several parallel attention sub-components in a transformer model, each learning to focus on different relationships within the input.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HEAD, the second word, while attention carries only light secondary stress. Say the -tion ending as 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Machine learning engineers and researchers use attention head when discussing transformer architectures, interpretability, or pruning. In papers and code the phrase is standard, while in casual team talk people often just say 'the heads' in plural. It is not a term for a person's mind or a physical part of anything.

distinctions.note: The mechanism is the general operation for weighing input relevance, while an attention head is one of several parallel components that implement it.
A layer contains several attention heads whose outputs are combined before passing to the next step.
A neuron is a single unit, while an attention head is a group of computations that produces a weighted combination of inputs.

examples.everyday: My coworker said one attention head in the model seems to track pronouns, which is kind of cool.
examples.professional: We removed the three least-used attention heads, and accuracy dropped by less than half a percent.
examples.analytical: Each attention head can learn a different relation, so interpreting one head in isolation can mislead us about the model's overall behavior.

nuance.analogy: Like several detectives searching the same crime scene for different clues, with their findings combined afterward.
nuance.etymology: The sense comes from the Transformer architecture introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need,' where 'head' names a parallel processing unit.
common_mistakes: Thinking an attention head is a person or a physical part of the computer; it is a set of mathematical operations within a layer.
Saying attentions heads with the wrong plural; the usual form is attention heads.

conversation.text: We found an attention head that consistently copies tokens that appeared earlier in the context.
Removing a surprising number of attention heads barely changed accuracy, which suggests a lot of redundancy.
Each attention head has its own query, key, and value projections, so it can learn a different pattern.

senses.definition: A yard to the rear of a house or similar residence.
A person's neighborhood, or an area nearby to a person's usual residence or place of work and where the person is likely to go.
An area nearby to a country or other jurisdiction's legal boundaries, particularly an area in which the country feels it has an interest.

core.definition: The yard behind a house, often used for relaxing, barbecues, or playing; also a nearby area close to someone's home.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BACK, and pronounce the second syllable as 'yard' with a clear, rhotic r. The vowel in 'yard' is the open 'ah' sound of the cot-caught merger, not a short a.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually evokes home, family, and everyday comfort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'backyard' for the private yard behind a house, as in 'We're having a barbecue in the backyard.' The phrase 'in our own backyard' means close to home or in our local area, often in a slightly worried way, as in NIMBY debates. In British English people may say 'back garden', so 'backyard' is the American form.

distinctions.note: Yard is the general word for an outdoor enclosed area, while backyard specifically refers to the area behind a house.
A garden is an area for growing plants, while a backyard is the rear yard, which may or may not include a garden.

examples.everyday: We're doing a barbecue in the backyard on Saturday, so bring your swimsuit.
examples.professional: The competitor's new product just launched in our backyard, so we need to respond before they take our customers.
examples.analytical: States often define their backyard as the region they consider vital to their security, which shapes their foreign policy.

nuance.analogy: Like an extension of your living room where the walls are trees and the ceiling is the sky.
nuance.etymology: Back and yard; yard comes from Old English geard, meaning an enclosure.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'back-YARD' instead of BAK-yard.
Using 'backyard' for the front yard, which is the area in front of the house.
Writing 'back yard' as two words in informal speech, though one word is standard in American writing.

conversation.text: The kids are playing in the backyard.
We're having a barbecue in the backyard on Saturday.
Our backyard is small, but it has a nice big tree.

senses.definition: One who bags.
A retail employee who bags customers' purchases and carries them to the customers' vehicles.
A touring motorcycle equipped with saddlebags.

core.definition: A store employee who puts customers' purchases into bags, often helping carry them out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'er' is an American r-colored vowel, so pronounce a clear r sound rather than 'bag-uh'. Keep the short a of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an entry-level service job without negative implications.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bagger' in grocery stores and other retail shops to mean the person who bags purchases. It is casual and common in everyday speech. You might say 'The bagger was really nice' or tip a bagger in some places, especially at larger stores.

distinctions.note: A cashier handles payment and scanning; a bagger packs the items after payment.
A stocker puts products on shelves, while a bagger works at the checkout and packs customers' purchases.

examples.everyday: The bagger at the grocery store double-bagged my eggs so they wouldn't break on the way home.
examples.professional: We're hiring baggers and cashiers for the new store opening next month, so please share the posting.
examples.analytical: The bagger role is often overlooked in discussions of retail labor, though it shapes the customer's last impression of a store.

nuance.analogy: Like a packing assistant who fills the box after the cashier has checked everything in.
nuance.etymology: From the verb bag, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'bay-jer' or with a long a vowel.
Using 'bagger' for a cashier, since the two jobs are different in American stores.

conversation.text: The bagger put the eggs on top, which was really thoughtful.
My son got a summer job as a bagger at the supermarket.
There's no bagger today, so I guess we're bagging our own groceries.

senses.definition: Portending evil; ominous.

core.definition: Showing or suggesting a threat or harmful intent, often through a look or expression.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'ful' is reduced to a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'fuhl' rather than 'full'. Keep the 'l' at the end clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests menace, dread, or hostility, and it is mostly used for looks, stares, or omens.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use baleful mainly in writing, storytelling, or formal descriptions of an unpleasant look or a sense of danger. In everyday speech, people usually say 'a dirty look' or 'a scary stare' instead. It is not common in casual conversation, so using it can sound dramatic.

distinctions.note: Menacing is common and directly suggests a threat, while baleful suggests a dark, hostile quality, often in a look or mood.
Ominous means suggesting future trouble, often in a sky, sound, or event. Baleful is more personal and focuses on hostile intent.

examples.everyday: The neighbor's dog gave me a baleful look when I walked past his yard.
examples.professional: The manager's baleful glance during the meeting made it clear that the proposal would not be well received.
examples.analytical: The novel's baleful atmosphere suggests that the institution itself, rather than any individual villain, is the source of the danger.

nuance.analogy: A baleful look is like a dark cloud over a sunny day: it does not strike immediately, but it signals trouble.
nuance.etymology: From bale (in the sense of evil or misery, from Old English bealu) plus the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'full' rather than the reduced 'fuhl'.
Using baleful for a simply sad or unhappy look, when it implies a threatening or hostile quality.

baleful.etymology: From Middle English *baleful*, *balful*, *baluful*, from Old English *bealuful*, which was equivalent to *bealu* + *ful*.

senses.definition: Belonging or relating to a baron or barons.
Suitable for a baron.
Impressive in appearance; stately; imposing.

core.definition: Relating to a baron, or grand and stately in a way fit for a baron's great house or estate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, ROH, and the ending is a quick 'nee-ul'. Learners often stress the first syllable or add an extra 'eye' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing grandeur; it can sound slightly ironic when describing something overdone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use baronial in writing or in talk about castles, estates, or history. It describes things like a baronial hall or a baronial fireplace. In everyday speech, say grand or impressive instead, since the word sounds literary.

distinctions.note: Regal describes a king, queen, or royal dignity; baronial describes the style or rank of a lesser noble.
Stately is a general word for dignified and grand; baronial adds a link to the baron class or manor-house style.

examples.everyday: The hotel lobby had a huge stone fireplace that looked like it came out of a castle.
examples.professional: The client wants the new lobby to feel baronial, with dark oak paneling and tall stone archways.
examples.analytical: The architect's baronial revival drew on medieval manor houses to project inherited authority.

nuance.analogy: A baronial hall is like a stage set for an old-fashioned lord's dinner: big, grand, and built to impress.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin baronialis, from baro (baron); the origin of baron itself is uncertain, possibly Germanic.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as BAR-oh-nee-al, which sounds unnatural
Confusing baronial, an adjective, with barony, which is the rank or territory itself

senses.definition: To clean oneself by immersion in water or using water; to take a bath, have a bath.
To immerse oneself, or part of the body, in water for pleasure or refreshment; to swim.
To clean a person by immersion in water or using water; to give someone a bath.
senses.example: We bathe our baby before going to bed; other parents do it in the morning if they have time.

senses.definition: To apply water or other liquid to; to suffuse or cover with liquid.
senses.example: She bathed her eyes with liquid to remove the stinging chemical.

senses.definition: To cover or surround.
senses.example: The room was bathed in moonlight.

senses.definition: To sunbathe.
senses.example: The women bathed in the sun.

core.definition: To wash yourself or someone else by immersing the body in water, or to give a person a bath.

pronunciation.tip: The verb has a voiced th, like the 'th' in 'breathe', while the noun 'bath' has a voiceless th. Say 'bathed' as one syllable, /beɪðd/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests care, cleanliness, or a calm, gentle immersion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'take a bath' or 'give the baby a bath' in everyday talk. They use 'bathe' more in formal, medical, or literary contexts, such as 'bathe the wound' or 'bathed in sunlight'. In casual speech, 'bathe' can sound stiff, so use it when you want precision or a warmer tone.

distinctions.note: 'Bath' is the everyday noun, as in 'take a bath', while 'bathe' is the verb for washing or immersing the body.
A shower uses water sprayed from above, while bathing means soaking or immersing the body or washing it in a basin or tub.

examples.everyday: I'm going to bathe the dog before we go to the park, so he doesn't smell like the lake.
examples.professional: The nurse will bathe the patient and check the incision before the doctor arrives on rounds.
examples.analytical: Leviticus 15 requires a person made unclean by a discharge to bathe in water, which shows that bodily washing had ritual as well as hygienic meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a river washing over a stone, bathing covers the whole body in water so that everything is cleansed or refreshed.
nuance.etymology: From Old English baþian, related to bæþ (bath).
common_mistakes: Saying 'take a bathe' instead of 'take a bath'
Pronouncing the verb with a voiceless th, as in the noun 'bath'
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew rāḥaṣ (רָחַץ), 'to wash'; Greek louō (λούω), 'to wash the body', and nipto (νίπτω), 'to wash a part of the body'. Leviticus 15:5 requires a person who touches a defiled bed to bathe in water and remain unclean until evening. 2 Kings 5:10-14 tells how Naaman is told to wash in the Jordan seven times. John 13:10 says that someone who has bathed needs only to wash the feet.

bathe.etymology: From Middle English *bathen*, from Old English *baþian* (“to bathe, wash”), from **baþōn*, from Proto-Germanic **baþōną* (“to bathe”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰeh₁-* (“to warm”).

senses.definition: The self-contained and fully realized being or existence of objects.

core.definition: In Sartre's philosophy, the complete, solid existence of things, which simply are what they are and have no consciousness or freedom.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SELF, with a secondary stress on BEE. In fast speech 'in' is quick and reduced, and the 'ng' in 'being' is a nasal sound, not 'bee-ink.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is an abstract technical term used in philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in philosophy classes and writing on existentialism, usually alongside being-for-itself. In everyday talk people would just say 'things' or 'objects.' Keep the hyphens in formal writing, and remember the French original is en-soi.

distinctions.note: Being-in-itself is the fully determined existence of objects; being-for-itself is the conscious, free existence of humans.
Existence is the general word; being-in-itself is Sartre's technical name for the self-contained being of things.

examples.everyday: A rock just sits on the trail, and in Sartre's terms that's being-in-itself, not someone making choices.
examples.professional: Our ethics panel used Sartre's distinction to explain why a machine is a being-in-itself while a user is a being-for-itself.
examples.analytical: Sartre argues that being-in-itself is complete and has no internal lack, which is why it cannot be free.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone: it is entirely what it is, with no gap between itself and its own nature.
nuance.etymology: From the French etre-en-soi, Sartre's term, literally 'being in itself.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with being-for-itself, which is the opposite concept
Thinking 'itself' implies selfishness; here it means the thing's own complete reality

senses.definition: A short invocation for help, blessing and guidance from God, said on behalf of another person or persons (sometimes at the end of a church worship service).
senses.example: to pronounce / give / say the benediction

senses.definition: In the Anglican church, the ceremony used to institute an abbot, analogous to the consecration of a bishop.
A Roman Catholic rite by which bells, banners, candles, etc. are blessed with holy water and formally dedicated to God.
Help, good fortune or reward from God or another supernatural source.

core.definition: A blessing, especially a short prayer asking God's blessing, spoken at the end of a church service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DIK. The middle vowel is reduced to uh, and -tion sounds like shun. Do not say "bene" as in "benefit."

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent; suggests a solemn blessing.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches, the benediction is the closing blessing, usually spoken by the pastor. Outside church, it can describe a warm closing blessing, sometimes with ironic grandeur. Most people say "blessing" in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Blessing is the common, general word; benediction is more formal and often the specific closing blessing.
An invocation opens a service by calling on God; a benediction closes it.
Grace is a prayer before a meal, or God's unearned favor, not the closing blessing.

examples.everyday: After the benediction, everyone stayed to chat over coffee in the fellowship hall.
examples.professional: Pastor Davis will offer the benediction at the end of the graduation ceremony.
examples.analytical: The Aaronic benediction in Numbers 6 shows how blessing functions as God's own act, spoken through the priest.

nuance.analogy: A benediction is the final handshake of a worship service, sending people out with God's blessing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin benedictio, from bene "well" and dicere "to speak," meaning "speaking well."
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "benefit."
Stressing the first syllable.
Saying it as ben-uh-DIK-tion with a hard t instead of shun.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew berakhah means "blessing." Numbers 6:22-27 gives the priestly blessing that Aaron and his sons pronounce over Israel. 2 Corinthians 13:14 closes with a blessing of the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Hebrews 13:20-21 also ends with a blessing that prays God equip believers.

traditions.view: The priest blesses the people at the end of the Divine Liturgy and other services, often making the sign of the cross with his hand, and the dismissal includes a blessing.
Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament is a devotion in which the priest blesses the people with the consecrated host in a monstrance. Blessings also close the Mass.
Most Protestant services end with a benediction by the pastor, often using biblical words such as Numbers 6 or 2 Corinthians 13:14. It is a pronouncement of blessing, not a sacrament.

benediction.etymology: From Middle English *benediccion*, from Ecclesiastical Latin *benedictio*, from *benedictus* (“blessed; well spoken of”).

senses.definition: In a benevolent manner.

core.definition: In a kind, generous way that shows goodwill toward others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the NEV syllable, and say the -nt-ly cluster smoothly without adding a vowel between the t and the l. The final syllable is 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a kind, sometimes condescending, attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use benevolently mostly in writing, such as in novels, reviews, or formal descriptions of how someone looks at others. In speech they would say kindly, gently, or nicely. It often describes a person in authority smiling at someone less powerful.

distinctions.note: Kindly is an everyday word and can be used in requests, while benevolently describes a formal, goodwill-filled attitude.
Generously focuses on giving, while benevolently focuses on the attitude behind the action.

examples.everyday: My grandpa just watched the kids argue over dessert and smiled benevolently.
examples.professional: The director watched the junior team's first presentation benevolently, offering help only when they asked.
examples.analytical: The narrator regards the villagers benevolently, though the novel's irony suggests a more complicated judgment.

nuance.analogy: Acting benevolently is like a grandparent watching a grandchild open a gift: pleased, patient, and wanting only good things.
nuance.etymology: Formed from benevolent with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as benevolantly or benevolently with an extra e.
Using it to describe objects or events, where good or positive is more natural.

senses.definition: To resist the urge to speak out, especially in order to avoid saying something inappropriate or likely to cause a dispute.

core.definition: To stop yourself from saying what you are thinking, usually because it would be rude or unhelpful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress tongue strongly and reduce your to yor, with a schwa-r rather than yoor. In fast speech, bite your links as bi-chur.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests self-control and tact.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to describe holding back a sharp reply, often at family dinners, at work, or with a rude customer. My brother said my cooking was bland, and I just bit my tongue is typical. A natural reply is Good call or I would have said something. Saying Bite your tongue! as an exclamation is playful and means Don't say that!

distinctions.note: Hold your tongue means the same thing but is slightly more formal and old-fashioned; bite your tongue is more common in everyday American speech.
Keep quiet simply means not speaking; bite your tongue implies you wanted to speak but chose not to.

collocations: bite your tongue and let it go

examples.everyday: My sister criticized my kids' table manners, but I just bit my tongue.
examples.professional: I had to bite my tongue in the meeting when the VP dismissed our validation results without reading them.
examples.analytical: A theologian who bites his tongue during a debate may preserve charity, but he may also suppress a necessary correction.

nuance.analogy: Like holding down the lid of a pot that is boiling over.
nuance.etymology: From the physical image of biting your tongue to keep words from coming out.
common_mistakes: Taking it literally, which sounds odd since the phrase means holding back words.
Confusing it with bite your lip, which means holding back an emotion such as worry or a smile.
Saying I bited my tongue; the past tense is bit.

conversation.text: When your in-laws start criticizing your cooking, just bite your tongue and smile.
I wanted to correct my boss in the meeting, but I bit my tongue.
"Maybe the project will fail." "Bite your tongue! We've worked so hard on it."

senses.definition: A section of split logs used as fuel.
A section of a railroad where the block system is used.
The distance from one street to another in a city or suburb that is built (approximately) to a grid pattern.
senses.example: The place you are looking for is two long blocks east and one short block north.

senses.definition: Interference or obstruction of cognitive processes.
senses.example: a mental block

senses.definition: A substantial, often approximately cuboid, piece of any substance.
senses.example: a block of ice; a block of stone

senses.definition: A chopping block: a cuboid base for cutting or beheading.
senses.example: Anne Boleyn placed her head on the block and awaited her execution.

senses.definition: A wig block: a simplified head model upon which wigs are worn.
A mold on which hats, bonnets, etc. are shaped.
A case or frame housing one or more sheaves (pulleys), used with ropes to increase or redirect force, for example as part of lifting gear or a sailing ship's rigging. See also block and tackle.
A set of sheets (of paper) joined together at one end, forming a cuboid shape.
senses.example: a block of 100 tickets

senses.definition: The perch on which a bird of prey is kept.
In Conway's Game of Life, a still life consisting of four living cells arranged in a two-by-two square.
A physical area or extent of something, often rectangular or approximately rectangular.
senses.example: a block of text; a block of color; a block of land

senses.definition: A joined group of four (or in some cases nine) postage stamps, forming a roughly square shape.
A discrete group of vines in a vineyard, often distinguished from others by variety, clone, canopy training method, irrigation infrastructure, or some combination thereof.
A logical extent or region; a grouping or apportionment of like things treated together as a unit.
senses.example: a block of data; a block of seven days; a block reservation

senses.definition: A logical data storage unit containing one or more physical sectors.
A region of code in a program that acts as a single unit, such as a function or loop.
A fixed-length group of bits making up part of a message.
A contiguous range of Unicode code points used to encode characters of a specific type; can be of any size evenly divisible by 16, up to 65,536 (a full plane).
senses.example: The "Specials" block comprises the sixteen codepoints from U+FFF0 through U+FFFF.

senses.definition: A yeargroup at Eton College.
A contiguous group of urban lots of property, typically several acres in extent, not crossed by public streets.
senses.example: I’m going for a walk around the block.

senses.definition: A cuboid or approximately cuboid building.
senses.example: a block of flats; a tower block; an office block; a toilet block; a shower block

senses.definition: A cellblock.
Something that prevents something from passing.
senses.example: There’s a block in the pipe that means the water can’t get through.

senses.definition: Any point on the board where two or more men rest, and consequently an opponent may not land.
A defensive play by one or more players meant to deflect a spiked ball back to the hitter’s court.
The portion of the movement where a gymnast pushes off the vault.
A temporary or permanent ban that prevents access to an online account or service, or connection to or from a designated telephone number, IP address, or similar.
senses.example: The Wiktionary page-blanking vandal was hit with an indefinite block.

senses.definition: The human head.
senses.example: I’ll knock your block off!

senses.definition: A portion of a macromolecule, comprising many units, that has at least one feature not present in adjacent portions.
An action to interfere with the movement of an opposing player or of the object of play (ball, puck).
A shot played by holding the bat vertically in the path of the ball, so that it loses momentum and drops to the ground.
The position of a player or bat when guarding the wicket.
A blockhole.
The popping crease.
(dated) A piece of hard wood on which a stereotype or electrotype plate is mounted.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To specify the positions and movements of the actors for (a section of a play or film).
senses.example: It was very difficult to block this scene convincingly.

senses.definition: To fill or obstruct (something) so that it is not possible to pass.
senses.example: The pipe was blocked by leaves.

senses.definition: To prevent (something or someone) from passing.
senses.example: A broken-down car is blocking the traffic.

senses.definition: To prevent (something from happening or someone from doing something).
senses.example: His plan to take over the business was blocked by the boss.

senses.definition: To bar (impose a ban on a person or bot, etc.) from connecting via telephone, instant messaging, etc. or from accessing an online account or service, or similar.
senses.example: I tried to send you a message, but you’ve blocked me!

senses.definition: To bar (a message or communication), or bar connection with (an online account or service, a designated telephone number, IP address, etc.).
senses.example: They’ve blocked all calls to international numbers.

senses.definition: To wait for some condition to become true.
senses.example: When the condition expression is false, the thread blocks on the condition variable.

senses.definition: To shape, stretch, or mold knitted items, hats, books (and book covers), shoes, etc.
senses.example: I blocked the mittens by wetting them and pinning them to a shaped piece of cardboard.

senses.definition: To shape or sketch out roughly.
senses.example: When drawing a scene, first block the main features, and then fill in the detail.

senses.definition: To experience mental block or creative block.
To reject or not play into one's scene partner during improv.
To impede (an opponent or opponent’s play).
senses.example: He blocked the basketball player’s shot.

senses.definition: To hit with a block.
To play a block shot.
(rare) To have sex with.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The stretch of a street from one cross street to the next in a city or town, used as a unit of distance.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short open /ɑ/ of 'hot' and 'cot', not a long 'oo' or 'uh'. The final k is clear and unreleased, with no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word used for directions and distances.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use block constantly for directions and distance, as in 'It's three blocks down on the left.' 'Around the block' means a short walk, and 'the block' can mean your neighborhood. British speakers say 'street' or 'road' in many of these cases, so 'blocks' is the American habit to learn.

distinctions.note: A street is the whole road; a block is the part between two cross streets.
A neighborhood is a whole area of a city; a block is one short segment within it.

examples.everyday: The coffee shop is just three blocks from my apartment, so I usually walk.
examples.professional: The new office is on the same block as the data center, so the commute is short.
examples.analytical: Researchers aggregated the data by census block to compare housing patterns across neighborhoods.

nuance.analogy: Like one square of a city grid drawn on a map.
nuance.etymology: From Old French bloc, meaning a log or chunk of wood; the city-block sense developed later in English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'two streets' when you mean two blocks; in American speech blocks are the usual unit of distance.
Pronouncing it 'blook' with a long vowel; the vowel is the short /ɑ/ of 'hot'.

block.etymology: From Middle English *blok* (“log, stump, solid piece”), from Old French *bloc* (“log, block”), from Middle Dutch *blok* (“treetrunk”), from **blok* (“log”), from **blokk*, from Proto-Germanic **blukką* (“beam, log”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰelǵ-*…

conversation.text: The restaurant is two blocks from my office.
Let's walk around the block while we wait.
A delivery truck is blocking the driveway.

senses.definition: A brag; ostentatious positive appraisal of oneself.
Something that one brags about.
senses.example: It was his regular boast that he could eat two full English breakfasts in one sitting.

senses.definition: A shot where the ball is driven off a side wall and then strikes the front wall.
To brag; to talk loudly in praise of oneself.
[with about or of] To speak of with pride, vanity, or exultation, with a view to self-commendation; to extol.
To play a boast shot.
To possess (a special and desirable quality).
senses.example: The hotel boasts one of the best views of the sea.

senses.definition: To dress, as a stone, with a broad chisel.
To shape roughly as a preparation for the finer work to follow; to cut to the general form required.

core.definition: To talk proudly about your own achievements or possessions, often in a way that annoys others. As a noun, a proud claim of this kind.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with an oh vowel that glides toward oo, ending in a clear st cluster. Do not drop the t, and do not say bowst, which rhymes with out.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting vanity and self-promotion, though neutral when a place or product boast a feature, as in the museum boasts a large collection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boast to describe people who loudly praise themselves, and the tone is usually mildly disapproving. In neutral speech, it can mean that something has a feature, as in the hotel boasts a pool. For everyday conversation, brag is the more casual and common word.

distinctions.note: Brag is more informal and common in everyday speech, often about small or personal things, while boast can be more formal.
Show off focuses on attracting attention through display, while boast focuses on what one says about one's achievements.
Claim is a neutral assertion, while boast implies pride and vanity in the assertion.

examples.everyday: My brother won't stop boasting about his fantasy football team.
examples.professional: Our new analytics platform boasts real-time dashboards, but we still need to validate the numbers before we rely on them.
examples.analytical: Modern thinkers often boast of reason's autonomy, yet the apostle asks what we have that we did not receive.

nuance.analogy: Boasting is like turning a spotlight on yourself and refusing to let anyone else step into the light.
nuance.etymology: Middle English bosten, of uncertain origin, meaning to boast or brag.
